{{DISPLAYTITLE:What has to be trusted}}
{{Technical|Lean theorem prover/System/The Lean kernel|Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Consistency and the metatheory}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

A proof that Lean accepts is not a proof that rests on nothing. It rests on a short list of
things that Lean itself does not check. This page gives the list, shows what two features of Lean
add to it, and says how independent checkers make it shorter. The list cannot be made empty, and
the page ends with what remains.

== Two questions, not one ==

Pollack divided the problem of believing a machine-checked proof into two questions. The first
is whether the proof really is a derivation in the formal system it claims to use. That is a
formal question, and a machine can answer it. The second is whether the theorem it derives
means what is claimed for it. That is an informal question, because one side of the comparison
is a human idea, and no machine can answer it.<ref name="pollack">R. Pollack, "How to believe a machine-checked proof", in Giovanni Sambin and Jan M. Smith (eds), ''Twenty Five Years of Constructive Type Theory'', Oxford University Press, 1998, chapter 11 (from p. 205); first issued as BRICS Report RS-97-18, Aarhus University, 1997. [https://doi.org/10.7146/brics.v4i18.18945 doi:10.7146/brics.v4i18.18945]</ref>

Lean's own guide to validating a proof draws the same line. It separates "does the theorem have a
valid proof" from "what does the theorem statement mean", and every check it describes speaks
only to the first.<ref name="refval">''The Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0, section "Validating a Lean Proof". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/ValidatingProofs/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/ValidatingProofs], consulted 14 October 2026.</ref>
The list below follows that division.

== The list ==

'''The Lean kernel is correct.''' Every proof is checked by the Lean kernel (see
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/The small trusted core|the small trusted core]]). If it had a
fault, it could accept a proof that is not one. Such faults have been found and fixed: work on
an independent checker written in Lean led to one being spotted and fixed.<ref name="l4l">Mario Carneiro, "Lean4Lean: Verifying a Typechecker for Lean, in Lean", arXiv:2403.14064, version 3, 14 September 2025. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14064 arxiv.org/abs/2403.14064]</ref>
Two more were reported and fixed in July 2026, in Lean 4.32.1 and 4.32.2: each could be used by a
program written for the purpose to make the Lean kernel accept a proof of <code>False</code>, from
which anything follows (see [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean since 2023|Lean since 2023]]). The
version of Lean this edition uses, 4.34.1, is later.<ref name="rn4321">''The Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0, "Lean 4.32.1 (2026-07-22)", release notes. [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/releases/v4.32.1/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/releases/v4.32.1], consulted 14 October 2026.</ref><ref name="rn4322">''The Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0, "Lean 4.32.2 (2026-07-28)", release notes. [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/releases/v4.32.2/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/releases/v4.32.2], consulted 14 October 2026.</ref>

'''Lean's logic is consistent.''' The rules of Lean's type theory, with its three standard axioms,
must not allow a proof of a contradiction (see
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/What the axioms are|what the axioms are]]). By Gödel's second
incompleteness theorem, a consistent system strong enough for arithmetic cannot prove its own
consistency, so this rests on an argument made outside Lean. One such argument, from 2019, showed
Lean's logic consistent provided that standard set theory, strengthened by assuming certain very
large infinite sets, is consistent; features added in Lean 4 mean that the argument no longer
applies directly to Lean as it now stands.<ref name="l4l" />

'''No other axiom has crept in.''' Anyone can add an axiom to Lean, and an unsound one proves
anything. The command <code>#print axioms</code> lists every axiom a theorem depends on, directly
or through the results it uses. Lean's guide says that only the built-in axioms
<code>propext</code>, <code>Classical.choice</code> and <code>Quot.sound</code> should appear;
any other name marks an unfinished proof, native evaluation, or an axiom that someone
declared.<ref name="refval" /> Pollack adds a point that is easy
to miss: the tool that lists the assumptions must itself be trusted, because nobody can read a
large proof to confirm the list.<ref name="pollack" />

'''The machine works.''' The checker runs on a processor, under an operating system, after a
compiler has turned its source into a program. Pollack placed all of these in a stack beneath the
checker, and pointed out that belief in a machine-checked proof therefore depends on empirical
knowledge of how physical hardware behaves, which belief in a proof on paper does not.<ref name="pollack" />
Running the check again on different machines and with different compilers makes it most
unlikely that a fault in the platform is the cause of an acceptance; it leaves a fault in the
checker itself untouched, which is why independent checkers matter more.<ref name="pollack" />

'''The libraries were written in good faith.''' A proof usually rests on imported definitions and
theorems. Lean's guide assumes that their authors were honest and declared no unsound
axioms.<ref name="refval" />

'''The statement is the right one.''' This is the second of Pollack's questions, and it is left to
people. See [[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Stating the right thing|stating the right thing]].

== What native evaluation adds ==

Lean is also a programming language, and some of its features let a compiled program stand in
for the Lean kernel's own computation. Lean's guide names two consequences. A proof by native
evaluation (the tactic <code>native_decide</code>, or <code>decide +native</code>)
depends on the correctness of the Lean compiler and of every definition marked
<code>@[implemented_by]</code>; and any such replacement in a library, made with
<code>implemented_by</code> or <code>extern</code>, becomes part of the trusted code, since it must
mean the same as what it replaces.<ref name="refval" /> The following lines
show why. The attribute tells Lean to run one function in place of another that is not the same:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def other (n : Nat) : Nat := n + 1

@[implemented_by other]
def same (n : Nat) : Nat := n

theorem same_five : same 5 = 5 := rfl

#eval same 5
#print axioms same_five
</pre>

Lean 4.34.1 proves that <code>same 5</code> is 5, runs it and prints 6, and reports no axioms:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
6
'same_five' does not depend on any axioms
</pre>

The theorem is still sound: the Lean kernel reasons about the definition, never about the program
that runs in its place. Trouble starts when a proof takes the running program's word. Continuing
the same file:

<pre class="lean lean-cont" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
theorem same_six : same 5 = 6 := by native_decide

theorem oops : False := by
  have h := same_five.symm.trans same_six
  contradiction

#print axioms oops
</pre>

Lean accepts this proof of <code>False</code>, built on purpose to show the danger, and
<code>#print axioms</code> prints:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
'oops' depends on axioms: [same_six._native.native_decide.ax_1_1]
</pre>

The axiom list is what gives it away. Since Lean 4.29.0, each computation asserted by native
evaluation enters as an axiom of its own,<ref name="refval" /> and a theorem that depends on one is
believed only as far as the compiler and every <code>implemented_by</code> beneath it are believed.
The project this wiki records refuses <code>native_decide</code> in its proofs altogether
(see [[Principia Machina/Lean transition|the move to Lean]]).

== Making the list shorter ==

An '''external checker''' is a second program, written separately, that reads a proof exported
from Lean and checks it again. It removes the need to trust the parts of Lean outside the Lean
kernel, which an exported proof no longer passes through, and, if its author made different
mistakes, the need to trust any one implementation of the checking rules.<ref name="tcl4">''Type Checking in Lean 4'', online book, chapter "Trust". [https://ammkrn.github.io/type_checking_in_lean4/trust/trust.html ammkrn.github.io/type_checking_in_lean4], consulted 14 October 2026.</ref>
Lean's guide describes its strongest procedure in these terms: the proof is compiled in a sandbox,
exported, and checked by the Lean kernel or by an independent checker, and the statement proved is
compared with a statement written separately, in a trusted setting.<ref name="refval" />
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Checking a proof again later|Checking a proof again later]]
describes these tools.

They have a price. A checker that reads exported proofs has no access to Lean's compiler, so it
cannot check a proof that relies on native evaluation; such proofs have to avoid it if that level
of checking is wanted.<ref name="refval" />

== What remains ==

Even at its strongest, the procedure leaves a list. Lean's guide gives it: that Lean's logic is
sound, that the tool joining the steps together is correct, that the sandbox holds, that no fault is
shared by every checker used, and that the trusted statement contains no human error and is not
presented in a misleading way.<ref name="refval" /> Two of these are of a different kind from the
rest. Consistency is a mathematical question, argued outside any checker. The statement is a
human question, settled by reading.
